The lighthouse keepers' last logbook

PART-ONE-MARKER The final logbook from the island lighthouse arrived at the county archive last week, wrapped in oilcloth and tied with the same frayed twine the last keeper used on every parcel he ever sent ashore.

Archivists expected weather notes and lamp hours, and they found those, but they also found forty years of small observations about birds, boats, and the slow habits of the people who rowed out with supplies.

The early entries are terse and practical, written in a hurried hand that suggests the keeper was writing while the kettle boiled and the lamp still needed trimming before the evening light came on.

Advertisement

PART-TWO-MARKER By the middle years the entries grow longer and warmer, and the keeper begins recording the names of the fishing boats that passed, the colour of their hulls, and whether their crews waved back from the deck.

There is a run of entries from one hard winter when the supply boat could not land for nineteen days, and the keeper describes rationing the tea with a precision that reads almost like a scientific protocol.

Several pages record the arrival of a lost racing pigeon that stayed for a month, ate crumbs from the windowsill, and was eventually carried ashore in a biscuit tin so its owner could collect it.

The later entries mention the automation survey, the engineers who measured every room, and the quiet realisation that the lamp would soon turn itself on without anyone climbing the stairs to watch it.

The last entry is a single line noting the wind direction and the state of the sea, followed by the keeper's signature, which is steadier than any other signature in the book and underlined twice.

Written by a staff reporter.

COMMENT-MARKER My grandmother delivered groceries to that island for years and always said the keeper wrote down everything, including how many biscuits she brought and whether the tin was dented on arrival.

I would happily read the whole logbook if the archive ever scans it, because entries like the pigeon one are exactly the kind of small history that never makes it into the official records.
